facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: Named as the viewpoint character at the start: “Alice was beginning to get very tired of sitting by her sister on the bank...”

facts.text: Is bored by her sister’s book lacking pictures or conversations.
facts.argument: “what is the use of a book... without pictures or conversations?”

facts.text: Falls for a very long time down the well but remains composed and considerate: examines cupboards and shelves, takes an empty “ORANGE MARMALADE” jar and carefully stows it instead of dropping it; talks to herself, imagines being thought brave at home, and recites schoolroom facts (miles to the earth’s centre, Latitude/Longitude) despite not really understanding them.
facts.argument: “the sides of the well… filled with cupboards and book-shelves… jar… labelled ‘ORANGE MARMALADE’… she… managed to put it into one of the cupboards”; “after such a fall… How brave they’ll all think me at home”; “I wonder how many miles I’ve fallen… four thousand miles… Latitude or Longitude… (Alice had no idea what Latitude was, or Longitude either)”.

facts.text: Falls for a long time down the rabbit-hole, dozing and musing about her cat Dinah and whether cats eat bats, before landing unharmed on a heap of sticks and leaves.
facts.argument: "Down, down, down... 'Do cats eat bats?'... thump! ... down she came upon a heap of sticks and dry leaves... Alice was not a bit hurt."

facts.text: After landing unharmed, she runs down a passage, hears the White Rabbit around a corner, then finds herself in a long, low hall lit by a row of lamps.
facts.argument: "down she came upon a heap of sticks... not a bit hurt... the White Rabbit was still in sight... she found herself in a long, low hall... lit up by a row of lamps."

facts.text: In the locked hall, Alice finds a tiny golden key on a glass table and a hidden small door that opens onto a lovely garden she cannot enter; she wishes she could shrink "like a telescope" and later finds a bottle labeled "DRINK ME."
facts.argument: "tiny golden key" on a glass table; a "little door about fifteen inches high" leading to the "loveliest garden" but she "could not even get her head through"; she wishes to "shut up like a telescope"; finds a "little bottle" with a label "DRINK ME."

facts.text: Drank from a bottle labeled “Drink me” (not marked “poison”) and shrank to about ten inches tall; she thinks she is “shutting up like a telescope,” plans to use this size to reach the lovely garden, and feels nervous she might shrink away entirely like a candle going out.
facts.argument: “No, I’ll look first … whether it’s marked ‘poison’”; “she was now only ten inches high”; “the right size for going through the little door … that lovely garden”; “it might end … in my going out altogether, like a candle.”

facts.text: Self-admonishing and imaginative; she gives herself stern advice, sometimes scolds herself to tears, once tried to box her own ears for 'cheating herself' in a solo croquet game, and enjoys pretending to be two people.
facts.argument: "Come, there’s no use in crying like that!"; she "generally gave herself very good advice" and "sometimes she scolded herself so severely as to bring tears"; she remembered trying to "box her own ears" and was "very fond of pretending to be two people."

facts.text: Finds a glass box with a small cake labeled "EAT ME" and decides to eat it to change size—either grow to reach the key or shrink to creep under the door—to get into the garden.
facts.argument: She forgot the little golden key and couldn't reach it; then "her eye fell on a little glass box" with a cake marked "EAT ME"; she says, "I’ll eat it... if it makes me grow larger, I can reach the key; and if it makes me grow smaller, I can creep under the door."

facts.text: After finishing the cake, Alice suddenly grows enormously—more than nine feet tall—striking her head on the hall roof; in her surprise she exclaims “Curiouser and curiouser!” and even forgets proper English.
facts.argument: “now I’m opening out like the largest telescope… Good-bye, feet!”; “she was so much surprised… forgot how to speak good English”; “her head struck against the roof… now more than nine feet high.”

facts.text: Alice takes up the little golden key and hurries to the garden door, continuing her effort to reach the garden.
facts.argument: “she at once took up the little golden key and hurried off to the garden door.”

facts.text: Cries so much that she creates a large pool of tears in the hall, about four inches deep and reaching half down the hall.
facts.argument: “she went on ... shedding gallons of tears, until there was a large pool ... about four inches deep and reaching half down the hall”

facts.text: Self-admonishes for crying and then questions her identity, wondering if she has changed since yesterday and asking, “Who in the world am I?”
facts.argument: “You ought to be ashamed of yourself... Stop this moment” and later “I wonder if I’ve been changed in the night?... Who in the world am I?”

facts.text: Picks up the White Rabbit’s dropped fan and gloves and fans herself because the hall is very hot.
facts.argument: “Alice took up the fan and gloves... she kept fanning herself ... as the hall was very hot”

facts.text: Alice doubts her identity, comparing herself to Ada and Mabel; she finds her recitations and knowledge scrambled.
facts.argument: “I’m sure I’m not Ada... I can’t be Mabel... four times five is twelve... London is the capital of Paris... I must have been changed for Mabel!”

facts.text: Alice recites a distorted poem about a crocodile welcoming fishes, noticing her voice sounds hoarse and strange to her.
facts.argument: She begins to repeat 'How doth the little—' but instead says verses about a crocodile; 'her voice sounded hoarse and strange.'

facts.text: Shrank rapidly to about two feet high when a fan she was holding caused her to shrink; dropped it just in time to avoid shrinking away altogether.
facts.argument: "now about two feet high" and "the cause of this was the fan she was holding ... she dropped it hastily, just in time to avoid shrinking away altogether."

facts.text: Fell into and swam in a pool of her own tears from when she was nine feet high; initially mistook it for the sea.
facts.argument: "splash! she was up to her chin in salt water"; "she soon made out that she was in the pool of tears which she had wept when she was nine feet high"; "she swam about."

facts.text: Has been to the seaside once in her life.
facts.argument: Parenthetical aside: "Alice had been to the seaside once in her life."

facts.text: Ran back to the little door to reach the garden, but found it shut again with the little golden key lying on the glass table as before.
facts.argument: "she ran with all speed back to the little door: but, alas! the little door was shut again, and the little golden key was lying on the glass table as before"

facts.text: Produced a box of comfits from her pocket and distributed them as prizes to the group; she also had only a thimble, which she handed to the Dodo when asked.
facts.argument: "pulled out a box of comfits... and handed them round as prizes"; "Only a thimble," said Alice; Dodo: "Hand it over here."

facts.text: Finds the prize ceremony absurd but remains polite, bowing and accepting the thimble solemnly.
facts.argument: "Alice thought the whole thing very absurd... she simply bowed, and took the thimble, looking as solemn as she could."

facts.text: Misinterprets the Mouse's 'tale' as its 'tail,' focusing on its bends and missing the story.
facts.argument: Alice: "It is a long tail, certainly... you had got to the fifth bend, I think?"

facts.text: In the White Rabbit’s house, she drank from an unlabeled bottle and grew rapidly until she filled the room, unable to get out the door.
facts.argument: "There was no label this time... nevertheless she uncorked it"; "before she had drunk half... her head pressing against the ceiling"; "As it is, I can’t get out at the door."

facts.text: After the little magic bottle’s effect finishes, she stops growing but remains enormous and wedged in the White Rabbit’s house (one arm out the window, one foot up the chimney), unhappy and unable to get out; she also reflects she’s in a fairy-tale, wishes for a book about herself and resolves to write one, carrying on a self-chiding conversation.
facts.argument: “she put one arm out of the window, and one foot up the chimney… Luckily… the little magic bottle had now had its full effect, and she grew no larger… very uncomfortable… There ought to be a book written about me… when I grow up, I’ll write one… ‘Oh, you foolish Alice!’”

facts.text: Alice shrinks by eating one of the small cakes formed from pebbles thrown through the window and escapes the Rabbit’s house into a wood.
facts.argument: “the pebbles were all turning into little cakes… she swallowed one… began shrinking… ran out of the house… found herself safe in a thick wood.”

facts.text: Alice seeks a way to grow back to a larger size and considers eating or drinking something to manage it.
facts.argument: “I’ve got to grow up again!... I suppose I ought to eat or drink something or other; but the great question is, what?”

facts.text: Currently very small—leans against a buttercup, fans herself with a leaf; a nearby mushroom is about her height.
facts.argument: “leant against a buttercup... fanned herself with one of the leaves”; “a large mushroom... about the same height as herself.”

facts.text: Admits confusion from frequent size changes and trouble remembering lessons/verses; tries to control her irritation with the Caterpillar.
facts.argument: Says being many different sizes is confusing; 'I can’t remember things as I used'; swallows down her anger.

facts.text: Recites 'You are old, Father William' at the Caterpillar’s request but says some words have come out altered; she speaks timidly and in a melancholy voice.
facts.argument: 'Alice replied in a very melancholy voice.' … 'Alice folded her hands, and began' … 'said Alice, timidly; “some of the words have got altered.”'

facts.text: Alice is currently three inches tall and finds the height wretched; she seeks to grow a little larger.
facts.argument: Alice: “three inches is such a wretched height to be.”

facts.text: Alice eats more mushroom bits, causing her body to shrink while her neck grows extremely long, allowing her head to rise above the treetops.
facts.argument: She eats “the other bit,” then finds her head free but with “an immense length of neck… like a stalk” above a “sea of green leaves.”

facts.text: Hesitantly identifies herself as a 'little girl' despite doubts due to her many size changes that day.
facts.argument: Alice: “I—I’m a little girl,” … “rather doubtfully, as she remembered the number of changes she had gone through that day.”

facts.text: Carries two pieces of the mushroom and uses them deliberately to control her size—nibbling alternately to return to her usual height, then shrinking herself to about nine inches to approach a small house without alarming its occupants.
facts.argument: “she still held the pieces of mushroom… nibbling first at one and then at the other… until she had succeeded in bringing herself down to her usual height… she… did not venture… till she had brought herself down to nine inches high.”

facts.text: Reaffirms her goal of entering the beautiful garden, viewing size control as half her plan and wondering how to gain entry next.
facts.argument: “Come, there’s half my plan done now! … the next thing is, to get into that beautiful garden—how is that to be done?”

facts.text: Laughs at the footmen’s tangled curls and retreats into the wood to avoid being heard; later approaches the door and knocks timidly, asking how to get in.
facts.argument: “Alice laughed so much… had to run back into the wood… Alice went timidly up to the door, and knocked… ‘Please, then,’ said Alice, ‘how am I to get in?’”

facts.text: Carries the Duchess's baby away to protect it, scolds its grunting, and releases it once it turns into a pig.
facts.argument: “If I don’t take this child away with me… wouldn’t it be murder to leave it behind?” / “Don’t grunt.” / “It was neither more nor less than a pig… so she set the little creature down.”

facts.text: Would like to play croquet with the Queen but has not been invited.
facts.argument: “I should like it very much,” said Alice, “but I haven’t been invited yet.”

facts.text: Before approaching the March Hare's house, she uses the left-hand mushroom to adjust her size to about two feet high.
facts.argument: "she had nibbled some more of the lefthand bit of mushroom, and raised herself to about two feet high."

facts.text: Leaves the Hatter and March Hare's tea-party in disgust, vowing never to return.
facts.argument: "she got up in great disgust"; "At any rate I’ll never go there again!... It’s the stupidest tea-party I ever was at"

facts.text: Finds a door in a tree, returns to the long hall, uses the little golden key and a piece of mushroom from her pocket to become about a foot high, and finally enters the beautiful garden.
facts.argument: "one of the trees had a door"; "Once more she found herself in the long hall"; "taking the little golden key"; "nibbling at the mushroom... about a foot high"; "at last in the beautiful garden"

facts.text: Shows boldness and lack of fear toward the card-court; she calls the Queen’s threat "Nonsense" and tells herself they are only a pack of cards.
facts.argument: "Nonsense!"; "they’re only a pack of cards ... I needn’t be afraid"

facts.text: Struggles to play the Queen’s croquet game: her flamingo mallet twists to look at her, the hedgehog ball crawls away, the ground is ridged, and soldiers move off, making it very difficult.
facts.argument: Her flamingo “would twist itself round and look up…,” the hedgehog “had unrolled itself… crawling away,” and soldiers kept walking off; she concludes it’s “a very difficult game indeed.”

facts.text: Wants to slip away from the chaotic croquet game without being noticed.
facts.argument: “She was looking about for some way of escape… wondering whether she could get away without being seen.”

facts.text: She proposes consulting the Duchess since the Cheshire Cat belongs to her.
facts.argument: Alice: “It belongs to the Duchess: you’d better ask her about it.”

facts.text: Alice imagines becoming a Duchess and resolves there would be no pepper in her kitchen, linking pepper to hot tempers and other flavors to moods.
facts.argument: “When I’m a Duchess… I won’t have any pepper in my kitchen at all… pepper… makes people hot-tempered… vinegar… sour… camomile… bitter… barley-sugar… make children sweet-tempered.”

facts.text: Uses a live flamingo as a croquet mallet, and expresses caution that it might bite when the Duchess suggests putting an arm around her waist.
facts.argument: "doubtful about the temper of your flamingo"; Alice replies, "He might bite"

facts.text: States she attended a day-school; learned French and music but not washing.
facts.argument: “I’ve been to a day-school… we learned French and music.” / “Certainly not!” (to ‘washing’)

facts.text: Compliments the song about the whiting; nearly says she has seen whitings at dinner before checking herself; is puzzled by the Gryphon’s shoe-polish remark and looks at her shoes, thinking.
facts.argument: "I do so like that curious song about the whiting!"; "I’ve often seen them at dinn—"; "Does the boots and shoes!"; "Alice looked down at them, and considered."

facts.text: Feels relieved the Lobster Quadrille is over before praising the song about the whiting.
facts.argument: "Thank you, it’s a very interesting dance to watch," said Alice, feeling very glad that it was over at last.

facts.text: Her attempt to recite a school verse twists into a lobster-themed parody ('’Tis the voice of the Lobster') because her mind is occupied by the Lobster Quadrille.
facts.argument: “her head was so full of the Lobster Quadrille, that she hardly knew what she was saying, and the words came very queer indeed:— ‘’Tis the voice of the Lobster …’”

facts.text: When questioned about turning out toes with a nose, she answers it’s the first position in dancing, though she remains puzzled and tries to change the subject.
facts.argument: “‘It’s the first position in dancing.’ Alice said; but was dreadfully puzzled … and longed to change the subject.”

facts.text: Has never been in a court of justice before; recognizes roles like judge and jury from books.
facts.argument: “Alice had never been in a court of justice before, but she had read about them in books ... ‘That’s the judge’ ... ‘that’s the jury-box.’”

facts.text: Begins growing larger again during the trial and decides to remain seated as long as there is room.
facts.argument: “she was beginning to grow larger again... she decided to remain where she was as long as there was room for her.”

facts.text: Called as a witness in the Hearts’ court; in her flurry, forgetting how large she has recently grown, she jumps up and tips over the jury-box.
facts.argument: White Rabbit reads “Alice!”; “she jumped up … tipped over the jury-box … forgetting how large she had grown in the last few minutes.”

facts.text: Refused to leave the court under the King's 'Rule Forty-two' and challenged its legitimacy, arguing it was newly invented and that if oldest it should be Number One.
facts.argument: "Well, I shan't go... besides, that's not a regular rule: you invented it just now." / "Then it ought to be Number One."

facts.text: Grows rapidly during the trial, becoming so large she is unafraid to interrupt the King.
facts.argument: "she had grown so large in the last few minutes that she wasn't a bit afraid of interrupting him"

facts.text: Wakes on the riverbank from a long sleep with her head in her sister’s lap and recognizes Wonderland as a "curious dream."
facts.argument: “found herself lying on the bank, with her head in the lap of her sister… ‘Oh, I’ve had such a curious dream!’”

facts.text: Regains her full size in the courtroom before defying the Queen.
facts.argument: “(she had grown to her full size by this time.)”

facts.text: After waking, she runs off thinking of her adventure as a wonderful dream.
facts.argument: "Alice got up and ran off... thinking... what a wonderful dream it had been."

facts.text: Upon waking, she explicitly frames her Wonderland experience as a dream, calling it 'a wonderful dream.'
facts.argument: "thinking... what a wonderful dream it had been."

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: Mentioned as sitting with Alice and reading a book: “Alice was beginning to get very tired of sitting by her sister on the bank...”

facts.text: Wakes Alice from her long sleep on the bank, listens to her recount the dream, kisses her, and tells her to go to tea.
facts.argument: “Wake up, Alice dear!” … “she told her sister… all these strange Adventures” … “her sister kissed her… ‘run in to your tea’”

facts.text: After Alice leaves, she sits watching the setting sun and drifts into her own dream, vividly imagining Alice and the Wonderland creatures around her.
facts.argument: "her sister sat still... watching the setting sun... thinking of little Alice... till she too began dreaming... the whole place around her became alive with the strange creatures"

facts.text: She fondly envisions Alice grown into a woman who keeps her childhood’s loving heart, gathers children to tell them strange tales—perhaps the Wonderland dream—and feels their simple sorrows and joys, recalling her own happy child-life and summer days.
facts.argument: “she pictured… how this same little sister of hers would… be herself a grown woman… keep… the loving heart… gather… other little children… with the dream of Wonderland… feel… their simple sorrows… remembering her own child-life.”

facts.text: Sitting with eyes closed, she half believes herself in Wonderland, yet knows opening her eyes will reveal ordinary reality (sheep-bells, a shepherd boy’s voice, farm-yard clamour, cattle lowing).
facts.argument: “she sat on, with closed eyes, and half believed herself in Wonderland… the rattling teacups would change to tinkling sheep-bells… the Queen’s… cries to the voice of the shepherd boy… to the busy farm-yard… the lowing of the cattle.”

summaries.text: Unnamed sister who sits with Alice on the riverbank reading a book without pictures or conversations.

Alice's unnamed sister, who reads quietly beside Alice on the riverbank, wakes her from a long sleep, listens to her dream, and encourages her to join tea. She serves as a grounding presence in Alice's whimsical adventures.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: Introduced as a talking rabbit with pink eyes who carries a watch and wears a waistcoat-pocket.

facts.text: Exclaims, "Oh my ears and whiskers, how late it’s getting!" while hurrying ahead of Alice.
facts.argument: "as it turned a corner, 'Oh my ears and whiskers, how late it’s getting!'"

facts.text: Returns splendidly dressed, carrying white kid gloves and a large fan, and hurries along muttering anxiously about the Duchess.
facts.argument: “the White Rabbit returning, splendidly dressed, with a pair of white kid gloves in one hand and a large fan in the other... ‘Oh! the Duchess... won’t she be savage if I’ve kept her waiting!’”

facts.text: Owns little white kid gloves.
facts.argument: Alice notices she had put on "one of the Rabbit’s little white kid gloves."

facts.text: Owns a neat little house marked with a brass plate reading “W. RABBIT”; has a housemaid named Mary Ann; anxiously searches for his fan and white kid gloves, fearing the Duchess will have him executed for losing them.
facts.argument: “on the door … a bright brass plate with the name ‘W. RABBIT’”; “Why, Mary Ann … fetch me a pair of gloves and a fan!”; “She’ll get me executed … Where can I have dropped them?”

facts.text: He returns calling for his maid and his gloves, and comes upstairs looking for “Mary Ann.”
facts.argument: “‘Mary Ann! Mary Ann! … Fetch me my gloves this moment!’ Then came a little pattering of feet on the stairs… Alice knew it was the Rabbit.”

facts.text: Calls for a subordinate named Pat to help outside his house and orders him to remove the arm at the window.
facts.argument: “Pat! Pat! Where are you?” and “go and take it away!”

facts.text: Present outside his house directing the crowd; his voice is heard ordering others to catch Bill after the ejection.
facts.argument: “then the Rabbit’s voice—‘Catch him, you by the hedge!’”

facts.text: Referred to by others as “the master” while coordinating efforts outside his house.
facts.argument: Voices: “the master says you’re to go down the chimney!”

facts.text: The White Rabbit escalates against the giant intruder in his house, proposing to burn the house and ordering a barrowful of pebbles that are then thrown through the window.
facts.argument: Rabbit: “We must burn the house down!” and later “A barrowful will do” followed by “a shower of little pebbles… at the window.”

facts.text: Seen among the Queen’s guests in the royal procession, talking hurriedly and smiling at everything, passing by without noticing Alice.
facts.argument: “among them Alice recognised the White Rabbit… talking in a hurried nervous manner, smiling at everything… went by without noticing her.”

facts.text: Serves as court herald/clerk during the trial, standing near the King holding a trumpet and a scroll of parchment.
facts.argument: “near the King was the White Rabbit, with a trumpet in one hand, and a scroll of parchment in the other.”

facts.text: Acts as court herald during the trial: blows a trumpet, reads the accusation from a parchment, and calls the first witness.
facts.argument: "The White Rabbit blew three blasts on the trumpet... unrolled the parchment scroll, and read..." then "called out, 'First witness!'"

facts.text: Acts as a procedural advisor during the trial, prompting the King to cross-examine an uncooperative witness.
facts.argument: White Rabbit: "Your Majesty must cross-examine this witness."

facts.text: Acts as court herald, fumbling over the list and reading out Alice’s name in a shrill little voice.
facts.argument: “Alice watched the White Rabbit as he fumbled over the list … the White Rabbit read out … in his shrill little voice, the name ‘Alice!’”

facts.text: Acts as court evidence-reader: presents a newly found paper and reads its verses aloud, putting on spectacles to do so.
facts.argument: "this paper has just been picked up" ... "The White Rabbit put on his spectacles" and read the verses.

summaries.text: A talking White Rabbit with pink eyes who frets about being late, checks a watch from its waistcoat-pocket, and darts down a rabbit-hole Alice follows.

The White Rabbit is an anxious, talking rabbit with pink eyes, known for his catchphrase, "Oh my ears and whiskers!" He wears a waistcoat, carries white kid gloves and a fan, and lives in a house marked 'W. RABBIT' with a maid named Mary Ann.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "Dinah was the cat."

facts.text: Alice describes Dinah as a dear, quiet cat who purrs by the fire, licks her paws and washes her face, is soft to nurse, and is 'a capital one for catching mice.'
facts.argument: "She is such a dear quiet thing... sits purring... licking her paws... such a nice soft thing to nurse... such a capital one for catching mice."

facts.text: Known for catching mice and eating small birds; Alice believes she could fetch the Mouse back.
facts.argument: Alice: 'Dinah’s our cat... such a capital one for catching mice... she’ll eat a little bird as soon as look at it!' and 'She’d soon fetch it back!'

summaries.text: Alice's pet cat, whom Alice affectionately worries will miss her; associated with a saucer of milk at tea-time and hunting mice (Alice even wonders if she eats bats).

Dinah is Alice's beloved pet cat, known for her quiet demeanor and skill in catching mice. Affectionately described as soft and nurturing, she enjoys tea-time with a saucer of milk and is thought to be capable of fetching back the Mouse.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: Mentioned by the White Rabbit: “Oh! the Duchess, the Duchess! Oh! won’t she be savage if I’ve kept her waiting!”

facts.text: Feared by the White Rabbit as capable of severe punishment (even execution) if displeased over lost items like his fan and gloves.
facts.argument: “She’ll get me executed, as sure as ferrets are ferrets!”

facts.text: Receives a royal croquet invitation from the Queen, delivered to her door by footmen.
facts.argument: “For the Duchess. An invitation from the Queen to play croquet.”

facts.text: Seen in her kitchen for the first time: sits on a three-legged stool nursing a baby amid smoke; she sneezes occasionally in the pepper-laden air.
facts.argument: "the Duchess was sitting on a three-legged stool in the middle, nursing a baby"; "Even the Duchess sneezed occasionally"

facts.text: Displays volatile rudeness and cruelty: snaps at Alice (“You don’t know much”) and, upon a pun about axes, orders “chop off her head!” She also calls the baby “Pig!” with sudden violence.
facts.argument: “You don’t know much,” said the Duchess… “Talking of axes,” said the Duchess, “chop off her head!”; “It’s a Cheshire cat… Pig!”

facts.text: Dislikes arithmetic, saying she can’t abide figures.
facts.argument: “Oh, don’t bother me,” said the Duchess; “I never could abide figures!”

facts.text: Reported to be under sentence of execution for boxing the Queen of Hearts’ ears.
facts.argument: White Rabbit to Alice: “She’s under sentence of execution.” … “She boxed the Queen’s ears—”

facts.text: She is in prison and is fetched to the croquet-ground by the Executioner at the Queen’s command.
facts.argument: “She’s in prison,” said the Queen… the executioner went off like an arrow and came back with the Duchess.

facts.text: On reappearing she is in a pleasant, affectionate temper toward Alice, calling her “dear old thing” and taking her arm.
facts.argument: “You dear old thing!” said the Duchess, tucking her arm affectionately into Alice’s.

facts.text: The Duchess habitually moralizes, insisting everything has a moral, and is physically intrusive with Alice, resting an uncomfortably sharp chin on her shoulder.
facts.argument: “Everything’s got a moral, if only you can find it” … she “squeezed herself up closer to Alice’s side,” “digging her sharp little chin into Alice’s shoulder.”

facts.text: Alice perceives the Duchess as very ugly.
facts.argument: “first, because the Duchess was very ugly.”

facts.text: Shows sudden fawning agreeableness toward Alice and a habit of attaching morals to everything she says, repeatedly prefacing remarks with 'And the moral of that is—'.
facts.argument: "who seemed ready to agree to everything that Alice said"; repeatedly says, "And the moral of that is—"

facts.text: She habitually moralizes—‘moral’ is called her favourite word—and she visibly trembles and falls silent when the Queen appears, then flees at the threat.
facts.argument: “the Duchess’s voice died away… in the middle of her favourite word ‘moral,’” and her linked arm “began to tremble”; she leaves immediately when threatened.

summaries.text: Unseen figure the White Rabbit anxiously references; he fears she will be angry if kept waiting.

The Duchess is an unseen character referenced by the White Rabbit, who fears her wrath over lost items like his fan and gloves. She is known for her potential for severe punishment, including execution, if displeased.

The Duchess is an unseen character in 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland,' feared by the White Rabbit for her potential wrath and severe punishments, including execution, over lost items. She receives a royal croquet invitation from the Queen.

The Duchess is an unseen character in 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland,' feared by the White Rabbit for her wrath and severe punishments. She is introduced nursing a baby in a smoky kitchen and receives a croquet invitation from the Queen.

The Duchess is an unseen character in 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland,' known for her volatile rudeness and cruelty. Feared by the White Rabbit for her wrath, she is first seen nursing a baby in a smoky kitchen and receives a croquet invitation from the Queen.

The Duchess is an unseen character in 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland,' known for her volatile rudeness and cruelty. Feared by the White Rabbit, she is first seen nursing a baby in a smoky kitchen and is under sentence of execution for assaulting the Queen of Hearts.

The Duchess is a volatile and cruel character from 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland,' feared by the White Rabbit. Known for nursing a baby in a smoky kitchen, she is under sentence of execution for assaulting the Queen of Hearts, yet shows affection towards Alice at times.

The Duchess is a volatile and cruel character from 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland,' known for nursing a baby in a smoky kitchen. Feared by the White Rabbit and under sentence of execution for assaulting the Queen of Hearts, she shows occasional affection towards Alice.

The Duchess is a volatile and cruel character from 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland,' known for nursing a baby in a smoky kitchen. Feared by the White Rabbit and under sentence of execution for assaulting the Queen of Hearts, she shows sudden affection towards Alice.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: “I’m sure I’m not Ada,” she said, “for her hair goes in such long ringlets”

summaries.text: Acquaintance of Alice distinguished by long ringlets; invoked by Alice as a point of comparison during her identity doubts.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: “I’m sure I can’t be Mabel, for I know all sorts of things, and she... knows such a very little!” and later "I must have been changed for Mabel!"

summaries.text: Acquaintance of Alice whom she considers less knowledgeable; associated with a poky little house, few toys, and many lessons.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: Alice swims toward a splashing creature in the pool and discovers it is a mouse that later speaks: “Not like cats!” after she says “Où est ma chatte?”

facts.text: Openly hostile to cats (says his family always hated them) and also averse to dogs; reacts by bristling/trembling or fleeing when these are mentioned.
facts.argument: "Our family always hated cats: nasty, low, vulgar things!..." and later "the Mouse was swimming away..." when Alice spoke of a dog that kills rats.

facts.text: Declares his family has always hated cats, and recoils from talk of cats and dogs (trembles, bristles, then flees).
facts.argument: "Our family always hated cats... Don't let me hear the name again!" and after dog talk "the Mouse was swimming away... making quite a commotion."

facts.text: Referred to with male pronouns.
facts.argument: "the Mouse, who was trembling down to the end of his tail"

facts.text: Attempts to dry the group by delivering a very 'dry' history lecture (William the Conqueror), taking charge with an important air and checking if it helps Alice.
facts.argument: "Ahem!... This is the driest thing I know"; proceeds with William the Conqueror and asks Alice, "How are you getting on now, my dear?"

facts.text: Claims its history is "a long and a sad tale" and begins narrating, prompting a tail/tale misunderstanding.
facts.argument: Mouse: "Mine is a long and a sad tale!" followed by Alice puzzling over its "tail" while it speaks.

facts.text: Easily offended; stops storytelling and walks away when slighted.
facts.argument: After Alice offers to 'undo' the 'knot,' the Mouse says, 'You insult me...' then walks off, refusing to finish its story.

summaries.text: A talking mouse swimming in the pool who slipped in like Alice; easily frightened by mention of cats and speaks in a shrill, passionate voice.

A talking mouse who slipped into a pool like Alice, easily frightened by cats and dogs. He speaks in a shrill, passionate voice and is openly hostile to cats, claiming his family has always hated them, often trembling or fleeing at their mention.

A talking mouse with a shrill voice, known for his fear of cats and dogs, often trembling or fleeing at their mention. He openly declares his family's hatred for cats and tries to take charge with dry lectures, like on William the Conqueror.

A talking mouse with a shrill voice, known for his fear of cats and dogs, often trembling or fleeing at their mention. He tries to take charge with dry lectures, like on William the Conqueror, but is easily offended and walks away when slighted.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: Mentioned through “her brother’s Latin Grammar,” which Alice recalls when deciding how to address the Mouse.

summaries.text: Referenced only via his Latin Grammar book; no direct appearance.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: Alice describes "such a nice little dog near our house... a little bright-eyed terrier... with such long curly brown hair... it’ll fetch things... sit up and beg... it belongs to a farmer... it kills all the rats... worth a hundred pounds."

summaries.text: A little bright-eyed terrier near Alice’s house; long curly brown hair; obedient (fetches, sits up, begs); kills rats; owned by a farmer who values it at a hundred pounds.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: “there were a Duck and a Dodo, a Lory and an Eaglet” among the creatures in the pool who swam ashore with Alice.

facts.text: Tends to interpret words literally and in terms of its natural habits, quipping that when it "finds" something it’s a frog or a worm.
facts.argument: Duck: "I know what ‘it’ means... when I find a thing, it’s generally a frog or a worm."

summaries.text: A duck among the creatures that fell into the pool; part of the wet, cross party that assembles on the bank after swimming ashore.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: “there were a Duck and a Dodo, a Lory and an Eaglet” listed among the creatures in the pool who swam to shore.

facts.text: Assumes a leading role, formally moves to adjourn for "more energetic remedies," and proposes a Caucus-race as the best way to get everyone dry.
facts.argument: Dodo rises solemnly: "I move that the meeting adjourn, for the immediate adoption of more energetic remedies... the best thing to get us dry would be a Caucus-race."

facts.text: Organized and arbitrated the Caucus-race: marked a roughly circular course, let everyone start/stop at will, then declared it over and judged that 'Everybody has won, and all must have prizes.'
facts.argument: "marked out a race-course, in a sort of circle"; "they began running when they liked, and left off when they liked"; Dodo cried "The race is over!" and said "Everybody has won, and all must have prizes."

facts.text: Solemnly presides over a prize-giving and personally presents Alice with a thimble as a prize.
facts.argument: "the Dodo solemnly presented the thimble" to Alice while the group cheered.

summaries.text: A dodo among the animals in the pool; joins the soaked group on the bank seeking to get dry.
Dodo, a prominent character among the pool animals, leads the group in a Caucus-race to dry off. Known for his energetic remedies, he seeks to organize and motivate others in their quest for dryness.

Dodo, a lively leader among the pool animals, organizes a Caucus-race to dry off. Known for his energetic remedies, he encourages teamwork and declares that 'Everybody has won, and all must have prizes' after the race.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: “there were a Duck and a Dodo, a Lory and an Eaglet,” and Alice argues with the Lory about age.

summaries.text: A lory (parrot) among the pool creatures; argues with Alice and turns sulky, insisting it is older and knows better but refuses to tell its age.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: “there were a Duck and a Dodo, a Lory and an Eaglet,” among the creatures who fell into the pool and came ashore with Alice.

facts.text: Dislikes pompous language and long words; tells others to "Speak English" and hides a smile after teasing the Dodo.
facts.argument: Eaglet: "Speak English!... I don’t know the meaning of half those long words" and bends its head to hide a smile.

summaries.text: An eaglet among the pool’s creatures; part of the wet group on the bank trying to get dry.

Eaglet, a young eaglet in a pool of creatures, prefers straightforward communication and often teases others, like the Dodo, by urging them to 'Speak English.' Part of a wet group on the bank, he seeks to dry off while displaying a playful demeanor.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: “an old Crab took the opportunity of saying to her daughter ‘Ah, my dear! Let this be a lesson to you never to lose your temper!’”

summaries.text: An old mother crab among the pool creatures; admonishes her daughter to keep her temper.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: “said the young Crab, a little snappishly. ‘You’re enough to try the patience of an oyster!’”

summaries.text: A young crab, daughter of the old Crab; speaks snappishly to her mother.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: “one old Magpie began wrapping itself up very carefully, remarking, ‘I really must be getting home; the night-air doesn’t suit my throat!’”

summaries.text: An old magpie among the pool birds; cautious and quick to make an excuse to leave when Dinah is mentioned.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: “a Canary called out in a trembling voice to its children, ‘Come away, my dears! It’s high time you were all in bed!’”

summaries.text: A canary with children among the pool birds; nervous and protective, ushers its brood away when Dinah is mentioned.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: The White Rabbit calls out, “Why, Mary Ann, what are you doing out here? Run home this moment, and fetch me a pair of gloves and a fan!”

summaries.text: The White Rabbit’s housemaid; unseen so far. The Rabbit mistakes Alice for her and orders ‘Mary Ann’ to fetch gloves and a fan.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: A new voice answers the White Rabbit: “Sure then I’m here! Digging for apples, yer honour!” and is addressed by name: “Pat! Pat! Where are you?”

summaries.text: Pat is a helper summoned by the White Rabbit outside his house; he addresses the Rabbit as “yer honour,” speaks in a distinctive dialect (e.g., “arrum” for arm), and is reluctant to obey orders to remove the arm at the window.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: Multiple voices refer to “Bill”—tasked to fetch a ladder and to go down the chimney; later identified by a “little feeble, squeaking voice.”

facts.text: Assigned to go down the chimney; described only as a small animal with a feeble, squeaking voice; kicked out and sent flying "like a sky-rocket," then revived by the crowd.
facts.argument: “Bill’s to go down—Here, Bill! the master says you’re to go down the chimney!”; “a little feeble, squeaking voice”; “up I goes like a sky-rocket!”; “Brandy now—Don’t choke him.”

facts.text: Said to have the other ladder and told to fetch it; also told to catch hold of a rope before being ordered down the chimney.
facts.argument: Voices: “Bill’s got the other—Bill! fetch it here, lad! … Here, Bill! catch hold of this rope.”

facts.text: Addressed by others as “lad” and “old fellow,” indicating he is male.
facts.argument: “Bill! fetch it here, lad!”; “So you did, old fellow!”

facts.text: Bill is injured or incapacitated after being sent down the chimney; later he is held up by two guinea-pigs and given something from a bottle.
facts.argument: “The poor little Lizard, Bill, was in the middle, being held up by two guinea-pigs, who were giving it something out of a bottle.”

facts.text: Serves as a juror in the Hearts’ court; his squeaky pencil is taken by Alice, forcing him to write with a finger that leaves no mark.
facts.argument: "One of the jurors had a pencil that squeaked... (it was Bill, the Lizard)... [he] was obliged to write with one finger... it left no mark on the slate."

facts.text: Bill is explicitly referred to as “the Lizard”; during the trial Alice accidentally puts him back head downwards in the jury-box.
facts.argument: “she had put the Lizard in head downwards” (Bill serving as a juror).

facts.text: At the trial, after the jury was upset, he was too overcome to write and only sat with his mouth open, staring up at the roof.
facts.argument: "all except the Lizard, who seemed too much overcome to do anything but sit with its mouth open, gazing up into the roof of the court."

facts.text: After the Queen throws an inkstand, he resumes writing using the ink trickling down his face, having found finger-writing made no mark.
facts.argument: “Bill had left off writing... but he now hastily began again, using the ink, that was trickling down his face.”

summaries.text: Bill is a small animal with a feeble, squeaking voice, part of the group outside the White Rabbit’s house. He is ordered to go down the chimney and is sent flying when Alice kicks from inside.

Bill is a small male animal with a feeble, squeaking voice, part of the group outside the White Rabbit’s house. He is ordered down the chimney, sent flying by Alice, and later serves as a juror in the Hearts’ court, where his squeaky pencil is taken.

Bill, also known as the Lizard, is a small male animal with a feeble, squeaking voice. He is ordered down a chimney, sent flying by Alice, and later serves as a juror in the Hearts’ court, where his squeaky pencil is taken, forcing him to write with a finger.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "An enormous puppy was looking down at her..." It plays with a stick, barks, and nearly overruns Alice before she escapes.

facts.text: Enormous compared to Alice; playful yet boisterous, barks hoarsely, chases a stick, and tumbles head over heels.
facts.argument: "An enormous puppy... yelp of delight... short charges at the stick... barking hoarsely... tumbled head over heels."

summaries.text: A huge, playful puppy relative to tiny Alice; yelps and barks hoarsely while chasing a stick, nearly bowling her over before she flees.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: Alice peeps over a mushroom and meets the eyes of a large blue caterpillar sitting on top, arms folded, smoking a long hookah; it addresses her.

facts.text: Curt and contemptuous in conversation; dismisses Alice’s size-change confusion, denies metamorphosis would feel odd for him, repeatedly demands 'Who are you?' and admonishes her to 'Keep your temper.'
facts.argument: Replies tersely: 'It isn’t' … 'Not a bit' … 'You! Who are you?' … calls her back to say, 'Keep your temper.'

facts.text: Commands Alice to recite a poem, deems her rendition 'wrong from beginning to end,' and pointedly asks what size she wants to be.
facts.argument: 'Repeat, “You are old, Father William”' … 'It is wrong from beginning to end' … 'What size do you want to be?'

facts.text: The Caterpillar is exactly three inches high and defends that height, rearing up angrily when Alice calls it 'wretched.'
facts.argument: “It is a very good height indeed!” … (it was exactly three inches high).

facts.text: Tells Alice that different sides of the mushroom alter size: one side makes you grow taller, the other shorter; then departs.
facts.argument: “One side will make you grow taller, and the other side will make you grow shorter.” … “Of the mushroom,” and then it was out of sight.

summaries.text: A large blue caterpillar who sits atop a mushroom, arms folded, smoking a long hookah. Speaks in a languid, sleepy manner, seems aloof, and begins by questioning Alice’s identity.

The Caterpillar is a large blue creature sitting on a mushroom, smoking a hookah. Known for his languid speech and aloof demeanor, he questions Alice's identity and dismisses her concerns, often demanding 'Who are you?' and advising her to 'Keep your temper.'

The Caterpillar is a three-inch tall blue creature, often found on a mushroom smoking a hookah. Known for his curt demeanor and iconic phrase 'Who are you?', he questions Alice's identity and advises her to control her temper, while revealing the mushroom's size-altering properties.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: A large pigeon flies into Alice’s face, beating her with its wings, and shouts “Serpent!” while talking with Alice.

facts.text: Obsessively guards its eggs from serpents; says it keeps watch night and day, has not slept for three weeks, and has tried nesting in roots, banks, hedges, and even the highest tree—yet serpents still threaten.
facts.argument: “I’ve tried the roots of trees… banks… hedges… but those serpents!”; “must be on the look-out for serpents night and day”; “I haven’t had a wink of sleep these three weeks!”; “taken the highest tree… they come wriggling down from the sky!”

summaries.text: A large, defensive talking pigeon that flies at Alice, beats her with its wings, and accuses her of being a serpent.

The Pigeon is a large, defensive talking bird that aggressively confronts Alice, accusing her of being a serpent. It obsessively guards its eggs, claiming to have not slept for three weeks while watching for serpents, despite its efforts to nest in various locations.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: “a footman in livery… otherwise, judging by his face only, she would have called him a fish”—he runs out of the wood and knocks at the door of a little house.

facts.text: Alice takes him for a footman due to his livery, though his face looks like a fish; he runs out of the wood and knocks loudly at the door.
facts.argument: “she considered him to be a footman because he was in livery: otherwise… she would have called him a fish” — he “came running out of the wood” and “rapped loudly at the door.”

summaries.text: A footman in livery with a fish-like face who runs from the wood and raps at the door of a small house.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: “It was opened by another footman in livery, with a round face, and large eyes like a frog… the other was sitting on the ground near the door, staring stupidly up into the sky.”

facts.text: Sits impassively at the Duchess’s door, gives unhelpful/philosophical answers, and intends to sit there for days; a plate from inside grazes his nose and he continues as if nothing happened; eyes set very near the top of his head; whistles after dismissing Alice to do anything she likes.
facts.argument: Replies “Are you to get in at all?”; repeats “I shall sit here… for days and days”; plate “just grazed his nose… exactly as if nothing had happened”; Alice notes “his eyes are so very nearly at the top of his head”; he “began whistling.”

summaries.text: A door footman with a round, frog-like face and powdered curls who serves at the Duchess’s house; repeats messages solemnly and stares up into the sky.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "the cook was leaning over the fire, stirring a large cauldron which seemed to be full of soup"

facts.text: Leans over the fire stirring a large cauldron of soup heavy with pepper; notably does not sneeze despite the pepper-laden air.
facts.argument: "the cook was leaning over the fire, stirring a large cauldron..."; Alice: "There’s certainly too much pepper in that soup!"; "The only things... that did not sneeze, were the cook"

facts.text: After removing the soup from the fire, she violently throws everything within reach at the Duchess and the baby (fire-irons, saucepans, plates, dishes).
facts.argument: “the cook took the cauldron of soup off the fire, and at once set to work throwing everything within her reach at the Duchess and the baby.”

facts.text: Appears as the next witness at the trial carrying a pepper-box; her presence causes sneezing near the door. She refuses to give evidence and claims tarts are made "mostly" of pepper.
facts.argument: "The next witness was the Duchess’s cook... She carried the pepper-box... people near the door began sneezing... 'Shan’t,' said the cook... 'Pepper, mostly,' said the cook."

facts.text: Disappears from the courtroom during the confusion of expelling the Dormouse.
facts.argument: “by the time they had settled down again, the cook had disappeared.”

summaries.text: The cook in the Duchess’s kitchen, leaning over the fire to stir a cauldron of soup heavy with pepper; notably does not sneeze despite the pepper-laden air.

The Cook, a character in the Duchess's kitchen, stirs a peppery cauldron of soup without sneezing. Known for her violent outburst, she hurls kitchenware at the Duchess and her baby after serving the soup.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "the Duchess was sitting on a three-legged stool in the middle, nursing a baby"

facts.text: Sneezes and howls alternately without pause in the peppery, smoky kitchen.
facts.argument: "the baby... was sneezing and howling alternately without a moment’s pause"

facts.text: Queer-shaped and hard to hold: throws out limbs like a star-fish, snorts like a steam-engine, and repeatedly doubles up and straightens; requires being twisted into a knot and held by right ear and left foot to nurse properly.
facts.argument: “held out its arms and legs in all directions, ‘just like a star-fish’… ‘snorting like a steam-engine’… ‘kept doubling itself up and straightening’… proper nursing was to ‘twist it up into a sort of knot’ and hold its ‘right ear and left foot.’

facts.text: Stops sneezing, repeatedly grunts while being carried by Alice, and then transforms into a pig and trots away into the wood.
facts.argument: “the little thing grunted… it had left off sneezing… This time there could be no mistake about it: it was neither more nor less than a pig… it trot away quietly into the wood.”

summaries.text: The Duchess’s baby, nursed in the smoky, peppery kitchen; sneezes and howls alternately without pause.

The Duchess's baby, a peculiar and hard-to-hold infant, sneezes and howls in the smoky kitchen. Known for its starfish-like limbs and steam-engine snorts, it requires a unique nursing position, twisted into a knot while held by its ear and foot.

The Duchess's baby is a peculiar infant known for its starfish-like limbs and steam-engine snorts. It sneezes and howls in the smoky kitchen, requiring a unique nursing position, and eventually transforms into a pig, trotting away into the woods.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: "a large cat which was sitting on the hearth and grinning from ear to ear"

facts.text: A large cat in the Duchess’s kitchen sits on the hearth grinning from ear to ear and, unlike most others present, does not sneeze in the peppery air.
facts.argument: "a large cat... sitting on the hearth and grinning from ear to ear"; "The only things... that did not sneeze, were the cook, and a large cat"

facts.text: renamed to 'the Cheshire Cat'
facts.argument: The Duchess identifies it: “It’s a Cheshire cat,” said the Duchess.

facts.text: Explicitly identified as a 'Cheshire cat' owned by the Duchess; noted for its broad, persistent grin.
facts.argument: “why your cat grins like that?” … “It’s a Cheshire cat,” said the Duchess.

facts.text: Appears suddenly, sitting on a bough a few yards away, and grins silently at Alice.
facts.argument: “she was a little startled by seeing the Cheshire Cat sitting on a bough of a tree a few yards off. The Cat only grinned when it saw Alice.”

facts.text: Also addressed as "Cheshire Puss" by Alice; responds by grinning wider, indicating acceptance of the address.
facts.argument: “Cheshire Puss,” she began ... it only grinned a little wider.

facts.text: Declares that everyone in Wonderland is mad, including itself and Alice; self-identifies as mad.
facts.argument: "Oh, you can’t help that ... we’re all mad here. I’m mad. You’re mad."

facts.text: Directs Alice toward a Hatter and a March Hare, asserting that both are mad.
facts.argument: “In that direction ... lives a Hatter ... in that direction ... lives a March Hare ... they’re both mad.”

facts.text: Says Alice will see it at the Queen’s croquet game today, then vanishes.
facts.argument: "Do you play croquet with the Queen to-day?" ... "You’ll see me there," said the Cat, and vanished.

facts.text: Appears good-natured but has very long claws and many teeth; Alice treats it with caution and respect.
facts.argument: “It looked good-natured ... still it had very long claws and a great many teeth, so she felt that it ought to be treated with respect.”

facts.text: Demonstrates fine control over disappearances: can vanish slowly starting at the tail and leave only its grin lingering; also remarks he 'thought' the Duchess's baby would turn into a pig.
facts.argument: "vanished quite slowly, beginning with the end of the tail, and ending with the grin, which remained"; "I thought it would," said the Cat, after Alice said the baby turned into a pig.

facts.text: Can manifest partially: first as a grin/mouth, then eyes, then the whole head; often appears as a disembodied head and chooses not to show the rest.
facts.argument: “she made it out to be a grin… as soon as there was mouth enough… Alice waited till the eyes appeared… the whole head appeared… The Cat seemed to think that there was enough of it now in sight, and no more of it appeared.”

facts.text: Defies the King’s order to be removed, replying, “I’d rather not.”
facts.argument: “I’d rather not,” the Cat remarked; after the King insists, “it must be removed.”

facts.text: Its disembodied head faded away before judgment; the King and Executioner then searched in vain for it.
facts.argument: “The Cat’s head began fading… by the time he had come back… it had entirely disappeared; so the King and the executioner ran… looking for it.”

summaries.text: A large cat in the Duchess’s kitchen, seated on the hearth and grinning broadly; unaffected by the peppery air (does not sneeze).

The Cheshire Cat, a large, grinning feline owned by the Duchess, is known for its distinctive, broad smile and ability to remain unaffected by the peppery air in the kitchen. It often appears and disappears at will, adding to its mysterious charm.

The Cheshire Cat, a large feline owned by the Duchess, is famous for its broad, persistent grin and ability to appear and disappear at will. It remains unaffected by the peppery air in the kitchen, adding to its enigmatic charm.

The Cheshire Cat, owned by the Duchess, is a large feline known for its broad grin and ability to appear and disappear at will. Often called 'Cheshire Puss' by Alice, it claims madness and directs her to the Hatter and March Hare, showcasing its enigmatic charm.

The Cheshire Cat, also known as 'Cheshire Puss,' is a large, grinning feline owned by the Duchess. It possesses the ability to appear and disappear at will, claims madness, and guides Alice to the Hatter and March Hare, embodying enigmatic charm and caution.

The Cheshire Cat, or 'Cheshire Puss,' is a grinning feline owned by the Duchess, known for its ability to appear and disappear at will. It embodies madness, guides Alice to the Hatter and March Hare, and is characterized by its enigmatic charm and caution.

facts.text: character introduced
facts.argument: “I must go and get ready to play croquet with the Queen,” the Duchess said.

facts.text: Host of a croquet game happening today, as referenced by the Cheshire Cat.
facts.argument: “Do you play croquet with the Queen to-day?”

facts.text: renamed to 'the Queen of Hearts'
facts.argument: The Hatter references “the great concert given by the Queen of Hearts,” clarifying the Queen’s identity.

facts.text: Hosted a great concert in Wonderland.
facts.argument: '...the great concert given by the Queen of Hearts...'
